newsitem.title: USA: Sources close to Fed say odds favor May rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Sources close to Fed say odds favor May rate hike.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is likely to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points next week in another bid to insure against potential overheating of the U.S. economy, according to sources close to the Fed.
"There is a very good chance the Fed will do another 25 basis points, and virtually no chance it will do 50 basis points," one source told Reuters.
A second source close to the central bank noted that U.S. financial markets are not yet helping the Fed restrain growth, indicating the need for another insurance move.

The Federal Open Market Committee raised the funds rate by 25 points to 5.50 percent in March. It was the first time in more than two years that the FOMC, which next meets on May 20, tightened credit to address the potentially inflationary strength of the economy. The Fed left the 5.0-percent discount rate unchanged in March.
The first source said that whether a funds rate hike would be accompanied by a discount rate increase "would be entirely at the discretion of the (Fed) chairman" Alan Greenspan.

"If you don't believe a fundamental change has taken place in the economy, you have to be wary about the numbers that came out," the source said, referring to the 5.6-percent rise in the Gross Domestic Product in the first quarter.
The source was also referring to April's 4.9-percent unemployment rate that pointed to very tight labor markets.
Analysts have cited the higher-than-expected growth in the U.S. labor force as a reason why tight labor markets have not yet translated into rapidly rising wages.
"That last report scored a point to the view the period of rapid labor force growth is over," the source added, noting the decline in the size of the workforce from March to April.

"Regardless of what is regarded as trend growth, a small deviation from trend growth results in a small inflation rise. We are moving further away (from trend growth) which means the risk for higher inflation," the source also said, while acknowledging the Fed is expecting a slowdown "from the clearly unsustainable" pace of the past two quarters.

"The question is when the slowdown will come. The answer keeps being postponed," the source pointed out. "The slowdown was supposed to come in the fourth quarter and Q4 came as a surprise on the upside. At this point, some of us are getting wary about confidently predicting the slowdown is imminent."
Private economists are forecasting a second-quarter slowdown as the large surge in inventories in the first quarter should subtract from subsequent growth.

"I would focus on the final sales number, up 3.9 percent, a pretty hefty number. Even if inventories do not contribute anything to Q2, another 3.9 percent GDP with no help from inventories would be very strong," the source added, stressing that the key to second quarter remains consumer demand.
The second source said the Fed's move in March had failed to spark any market restraint and that more tightening was necessary.
"It's a situation where the stock market is beckoning you, the Japanese are taking care of the dollar," the source said.
The rally in U.S. stocks is likely to contribute to higher spending, while a weaker dollar would keep U.S. exports competitive, also adding to growth.
The second source further noted long-term market interests are roughly where they were before the March tightening, with no significant change in credit availability.
"The only thing that would make the Fed pause is if we get a lot more slowdown here. It's the third and fourth quarter that are at issue here," the source stressed.
